title: Enterprise prospect kit: positioning, competitive briefs, pricing guidance, case studies, security FAQ
author: Aisha Patel
content:
Overview

Purpose: This document is a single-page enterprise prospect kit meant for AEs and SEs engaged with mid-market and enterprise buyers. It consolidates positioning and messaging, short competitive briefs, pitch-deck guidance, recommended pricing/packaging approaches, representative case studies, and a security FAQ to accelerate deal motion and reduce review cycles.

Use: Link this doc from opportunity playbooks and include the Pitch Deck Checklist (section below) as the default presentation skeleton for customer meetings.

Core value proposition (one-liner)
- Redwood Inference: A production-first inference platform that delivers predictable latency, lower unit costs, and secure deployment options across hosted, dedicated, and private environments.

Key positioning pillars (3–4 bullets)
1) Production-first economics: Optimize token cost and latency with batching, KV/prefix caching, and quantization profiles—delivers measurable per-call savings compared to single-endpoint hosting.
2) Deployment flexibility: Same API and tooling across Hosted API, Dedicated (reserved GPU pools), and Private (VPC/on-prem) deployments—customers avoid re-architecting as requirements change.
3) Reliability and graceful degradation: Smart routing, model fallbacks, and SLA-backed Dedicated plans reduce operational risk for customer-facing applications.
4) Developer productivity: Fast SDKs, eval tooling, and first-class observability reduce time to production and mean fewer regressions during model updates.

Messaging by buyer persona
- Product/Engineering (primary): Focus on predictable latency, end-to-end observability (token-level cost + latency traces), simple SDKs, and rollout controls (canary/A-B/automatic fallback). Include performance numbers from perf profile when available.
- Platform/Infra: Emphasize Dedicated and Private options, autoscaling policies, network controls (VPC peering, private endpoints), KMS integration, and capacity planning support.
- Security/Compliance: Highlight audit logs, customer-managed KMS/HSM, SOC2/ISO readiness, data residency options, and on-prem packaging for regulated workloads.
- Finance/Procurement: Present predictable committed spend for Dedicated, detailed unit economics showing cost savings from batching/caching, and clear add-ons/overage mechanics.

Competitive brief (summary + battlecards)
- Competitors covered: OpenAI (hosted API), Anthropic, Cloud ML endpoints (AWS SageMaker/Vertex AI hosted endpoints), Self-hosted runtimes (internal infra or third-party runtimes).

Competitive summary table:
| Competitor | Primary risk for buyer | Redwood differentiation | AE talking points |
|---|---:|---|---|
| OpenAI | Limited hosting flexibility; enterprise SLAs require add-ons; single-hosted model variants | Deployment flexibility (Dedicated/Private); deterministic cost controls and model routing policies | "If you need private deployment or predictable committed capacity, Redwood avoids re-architecting later." |
| Anthropic | Similar hosted experience; enterprise features still maturing for many buyers | Performance/tuning playbooks, quantization profiles, and Dedicated GPU pools | "We provide practical cost/latency controls and an ops story for production serving." |
| Cloud ML endpoints (SageMaker/Vertex) | High ops overhead; inconsistent model runtime performance; custom engineering required | Turn-key runtime optimized for inference (KV cache, batching, kernel selection) and lower engineering lift | "We manage the inference runtime so your team focuses on product, not kernels and autoscaling." |
| Self-hosted runtimes (open-source) | Heavy operational burden and expertise required, risk of regressions | Unified control plane, observability, SLO-driven fallbacks, and optional Private install | "Get the benefits of a managed inference runtime without sacrificing control or security." |

Competitive battlecard guidance (quick rebuttals)
- If buyer says "OpenAI has the best models": acknowledge model quality, then pivot: "We integrate model catalog options (including compatible Open models) and provide deterministic serving and fallbacks that make the app reliable at scale."
- If buyer claims "we can self-host cheaper": ask about long-term TCO including hiring/tuning kernels, reliability engineering, and time to market; present three-year TCO example (see Pricing Guidance).

Pitch deck checklist (recommended slide order)
1) Title + one-line positioning (use core value proposition)
2) Agenda + buyer-centric outcomes
3) Current state & pain (latency, cost, reliability, compliance gaps)
4) Redwood solution overview (runtime + control plane + deployment modes)
5) Architecture diagram for the relevant mode (Hosted/Dedicated/Private)
6) Measured performance examples (latency & cost) and SLOs we can commit to
7) Pricing & packaging options (pilot → reserved → enterprise)
8) Customer case studies with metrics (latency improvement, cost savings, defect reduction)
9) Security & compliance summary (SOC2, KMS, audit logging, on-prem option)
10) Proposed next steps & success criteria (POC plan, timeline, decision gates)

Pitch deck slide tips
- Use concrete numbers: e.g., "Average 95th percentile latency 120ms for 1k token requests on Dedicated N GPUs" or "20–40% unit cost reduction vs naive single-VM hosting". Always annotate measurement methodology.
- Include a simplified architecture diagram per deployment mode.
- Provide a one-page rollout plan for the POC: scope, data residency, model selection, success metrics, and timeline.

Pricing guidance (recommended packaging and scripts)
- Pilot (proof-of-concept, 4–8 weeks):
  - Typical configuration: Hosted API with 1–2 dev seats, sample traffic, lightweight observability.
  - Pricing: usage-based (per-token) with free pilot credits and short-term trial SLA.
  - Close criteria: performance within agreed threshold (p95 latency target), quality acceptance, integration of observability hooks.
- Reserved (Dedicated) for production:
  - Typical configuration: Reserved GPU pool (N GPUs), autoscaling policy, prioritized routing.
  - Pricing model: monthly reserved capacity + overage billing for burst. Include one-time onboarding fee for configuration and on-call runbook creation.
  - Sales script: "For predictable business-critical throughput we recommend reserved capacity; we’ll size based on your request distribution and SLA target."
- Private/On-prem (large regulated customers):
  - Pricing: enterprise license + support tier + optionally a managed private control plane. Integrations (KMS, SIEM) billed as professional services.
  - Contracting note: include statements on data residency, SLOs, and upgrade windows in contract annex.

Representative pricing table (illustrative)
| Package | Billing type | Typical buyer size | Notes |
|---|---|---:|---|
| Pilot | Usage (per-token) + credits | SMB to mid-market | Low friction, fast POC |
| Dedicated Small | Monthly reserved (4–8 GPUs) | Growing product teams | SLA-backed; lower per-token cost |
| Dedicated Large | Monthly reserved (16+ GPUs) | Enterprise | Priority capacity, dedicated support |
| Private | License + support + PS | Regulated/enterprise | On-prem or VPC; custom SLAs |

Three-year TCO example (talking points)
- Provide a one-page example comparing: (A) internal self-hosted inference (engineer ops cost + GPU cost + incident risk) vs (B) Redwood Dedicated (reserved + lower ops burden). Use seller-provided inputs for request volume and latency targets; typical outcome: Redwood shows lower effective ops headcount and lower unplanned downtime risk.

Case studies (short, anonymized examples)
1) Fintech Analytics Platform (Mid-market) — Outcome highlights:
- Challenge: High tail latency during peak trading windows and unstable model rollouts causing customer-facing errors.
- Redwood solution: Migrated to Dedicated with autoscaling and prefix caching; configured canary rollouts + automatic fallback.
- Results: 95th percentile latency reduced from 380ms to 120ms; production incidents related to model updates reduced by 90%; estimated token cost savings of 28% through batching and caching.

2) Healthcare SaaS (Regulated enterprise) — Outcome highlights:
- Challenge: Data residency and audit requirements prevented use of public hosted endpoints.
- Redwood solution: Private deployment (VPC) with customer-managed KMS and audit log integration into SIEM.
- Results: Successful SOC2-aligned engagement; secure on-prem inference allowed a new product line to launch in an EU market within 5 months; procurement signed a 3-year enterprise license.

Security FAQ for prospects (short answers)
Q: Where is customer data stored and how long is it retained?
A: For Hosted API we retain logs per configured retention policy (default 30 days) and provide configurable retention windows. Dedicated and Private deployments support customer-controlled retention; on-prem deployments keep data in-customer.

Q: Do you support customer-managed KMS / HSM?
A: Yes. Dedicated and Private customers can configure KMS key usage for encryption-at-rest and TLS certs. For Hosted API we support integration with major cloud KMS providers for enterprise customers.

Q: What compliance certifications do you have?
A: Redwood maintains SOC2 Type II and ISO 27001 readiness artifacts. We provide compliance packs and can support customer audits for enterprise engagements.

Q: How do you prevent model-data leakage across tenants?
A: The control plane enforces per-tenant isolation, and Dedicated pools can be single-tenant. We also provide model-variant pinning and KV-prefix isolation to avoid inadvertent cross-tenant cache reuse.

Q: What logging/audit capabilities are available?
A: Token-level request logs, model version and routing metadata, and built-in integration hooks for SIEMs (via syslog/forwarder and S3 exports).

Q: How are security incidents handled?
A: We follow our incident-response process with initial triage, customer notification within SLA windows, and post-incident reports. For enterprise customers we offer an optional 24/7 incident hotline and runbook alignment.

  3) Propose a Pilot with clear success metrics and timeline (4–8 weeks).
